reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because it promotes purported free AFK Arena diamonds through a hack and directs viewers to FOXYCHEATS.COM. It asks viewers to enter a username, select a platform, download apps, answer questions, and repeat the process to participate.

citations.quote: AFK Arena Hack :face screaming in fear: How to Get FREE Diamonds :high voltage:️ Android and iPhone
Found the site online which I will link down below
all I did was enter my username I selected the platform and. Then all I had to do was download some apps and answer some questions
I recommend you guys do the same and I highly highly recommend them
Yes it is a hundred percent free and yes it's a hundred percent real

opening.argument: The available evidence does not establish deceptive solicitation. The speaker describes a personal process and says it worked, but the material does not show a payment demand, a guaranteed financial return, or any request for sensitive credentials. The claim can reasonably be understood as an account of the creator’s experience, while viewers remain able to research the linked site independently. Even the strongest language is limited to the speaker’s own assurance that the offer was free and real, not proof that every viewer will receive the same result. The evidence therefore supports caution and independent verification rather than a definitive scam finding.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution’s description identifies a link and a sequence of actions, but those facts alone do not establish deception. Entering a username and selecting a platform are not shown to be credential theft, and downloading apps or answering questions is not shown to involve payment or loss. The title’s use of “Hack” describes the advertised method, but does not prove that the creator knowingly made a false claim.

citations.quote: AFK Arena Hack :face screaming in fear: How to Get FREE Diamonds :high voltage:️ Android and iPhone

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of an explicit payment request does not resolve the core issue. The video presents a purported game-asset acquisition method as “a hundred percent” real and free, then encourages viewers to repeat it. The speaker’s assertion that it worked is only an unsupported personal claim; it does not demonstrate that the site delivered diamonds or that the process was safe.

opening.argument: This is most plausibly a tutorial or demonstration of an online process. The speaker explains how he located the site, what inputs he selected, and what tasks he completed, while describing the outcome from his own experience. That instructional structure is consistent with operational guidance: viewers are told what the creator did, rather than shown a demand for money or a scheme involving recruiting others. The on-screen presentation is also a direct presenter segment, and the ending asks viewers to engage with the channel, which is ordinary video publishing behavior. The evidence supports classifying the central activity as explaining a technology-related process.

rebuttal.rebuttal: Calling it a tutorial does not make the subject a scam. The speaker explains a repeatable process in first person and says he is confirming answers viewers requested. Nothing in the supplied material shows a fabricated result, a monetary charge, or a demand that viewers recruit anyone. The website overlay identifies the subject of the demonstration, but does not by itself establish fraudulent intent.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The instructional format is precisely what makes the promotion actionable. The title advertises a hack for free diamonds, the speaker directs viewers to an external site, and he tells them to perform app downloads and questions. Those steps are not evidence of a legitimate educational tool; they are the mechanism offered in place of proof that any game assets were delivered.

opening.argument: The material can also be read as promotion of an ordinary online service or referral process, not a classic scam mechanism. The creator describes visiting a site and completing routine digital tasks, but the evidence does not show a deposit, an investment, a guaranteed cash return, a downline, or a request for banking information. It also does not establish that the creator charges viewers or receives compensation for referrals. The advertised benefit concerns in-game diamonds, and the described steps are free from the viewer’s perspective. Without evidence of financial extraction or credential abuse, the content fits ordinary service promotion more closely than a proven scam.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The prosecution identifies a purported hack and a website, but it does not identify a payment, investment, recurring charge, or promised cash return. The described process uses a username, platform selection, apps, and questions; the supplied evidence does not show that these are credentials or that they caused loss. A recommendation and a link are compatible with promoting a free online service.
